client: I just feel so empty since my dad passed away. Everyone keeps telling me to "get back out there" and socialize, but when I'm with friends now, I just feel this weird distance between us. I don't even know if talking about it will help - it's not like it'll bring him back.
therapist:
It sounds like you're carrying a deep sense of loss, and the pressure to "move on" from others might be making you feel even more isolated. That distance you're describing with friends—could it be that you're needing space to grieve in your own way, rather than being expected to act a certain way?  

What comes up for you when you imagine giving yourself permission to feel this loss without any expectations from others?

client: I guess I just feel like I *should* be over it by now, you know? Everyone else seems to think so. When you say "permission to feel," part of me wants that, but another part is scared that if I really let myself grieve, I'll just fall apart completely. I've been holding it together by keeping busy, and the idea of stopping that terrifies me.
therapist:
It makes so much sense that you're afraid of what might happen if you stop keeping busy—it sounds like that’s been your way of protecting yourself from feeling overwhelmed. But I wonder if holding it together so tightly might actually be making the loneliness feel heavier?  

What do you think would happen if you let yourself feel just *one* small piece of the grief, rather than all of it at once?

client:
I don't know... letting myself feel even a little bit of that grief sounds terrifying. What if I start crying and can't stop? Last time that happened I had to cancel my whole day because I couldn't pull myself together. 

But you're right that the loneliness feels worse when I'm exhausted from staying busy all the time. It's just hard to imagine finding a middle ground.
therapist:
It sounds like you're caught between two fears—the exhaustion of running from grief and the overwhelm of facing it head-on. That canceling your day after crying makes me wonder: what if "falling apart" isn't a failure, but your heart asking for the space it needs?  

Could we explore what a gentler, more manageable approach might look like—maybe setting aside just 10 minutes where you *don't* have to "pull yourself together"?

client:
I get what you're saying about needing space to grieve, but I'm scared that if I actually let myself feel it for even 10 minutes, I won't be able to stop. Last time I cried, I couldn't function for days. 

The idea of scheduling time to fall apart feels... weirdly clinical? Like I'm putting my grief in a box when it doesn't work that way. What if I open the floodgates and can't close them again?
therapist:
I hear how terrifying that floodgate metaphor feels—like grief could drown you if you give it any opening. It makes sense that scheduling it feels too rigid when your loss is anything but orderly.  

What if instead of "scheduling grief," we thought of it as noticing when small moments of sadness arise naturally—like pausing when a memory comes up, rather than pushing it away? Would that feel less overwhelming to acknowledge in those tiny moments?

client: I guess that makes sense in theory, but what if those "small moments" turn into hours? Last week I saw my mom's favorite flowers at the grocery store and completely broke down in the parking lot. I couldn't stop crying long enough to drive home. That doesn't feel small or manageable at all.
therapist:
That parking lot moment sounds so raw and overwhelming—like the grief ambushed you completely. When those waves hit that hard, it makes perfect sense that "small moments" would feel impossible to trust.  

I'm wondering if right now, rather than trying to control the grief, we could focus on how you might care for yourself *after* those big waves? What would feel like true support when the tears do come—even if they last hours?

client:
I don't know... when the grief hits that hard, it feels like nothing helps. Even the idea of self-care afterwards makes me feel exhausted. Like I'm supposed to perform recovery instead of just feeling what I feel. 

Sometimes I just sit in my car for hours crying, and the thought of making tea or doing breathing exercises seems ridiculous in comparison to the pain. It's not that I don't want to feel better - it's that the sadness feels too big for those small things to matter.
therapist:
I hear how exhausting it feels to even *consider* self-care when the pain is that immense—like putting a bandaid on an ocean. You're absolutely right that no cup of tea could possibly match the scale of this loss, and the expectation to "do something" afterward might just add another layer of heaviness.  

When you're sitting in your car with all that sadness, what if the only "care" was simply acknowledging: *This is how big my love for him was*? No fixes, no tasks—just letting the tears be what they are?

client:
That actually makes me cry just hearing you say it. I've been trying so hard to push the grief away because it feels unbearable, but maybe that's making it worse. It's just... when I let myself really feel how much I miss him, it's like I'll drown in it. 

I don't know if I can handle sitting with that pain without completely falling apart. What if the sadness never stops once I start letting it in?
therapist:
It sounds like you're standing at the edge of that pain, terrified that if you take one step closer, you'll lose yourself in it completely. That fear makes so much sense—grief can feel like an ocean with no shore in sight.  

But I wonder if pushing it away might be like holding your breath underwater, exhausting you more than the tears themselves? What if *falling apart* isn't failure, but the way your heart rebuilds itself around this loss?

client:
I get what you're saying about not pushing the grief away, but the idea of letting myself fall apart completely terrifies me. What if I can't put myself back together again? I've seen people get stuck in their pain and never really recover, and I don't want that to be me. 

It's just...when I start to feel it coming, my chest gets so tight and my thoughts race—it feels like drowning. How am I supposed to trust that this won't destroy me?
therapist:
That tightness in your chest and racing thoughts show just how physically overwhelming this grief feels—like your whole body is bracing against a storm. It makes perfect sense that you'd fear getting lost in it, especially when you've seen others struggle to find their way back.  

What if we thought of this not as "falling apart forever," but as your heart learning to carry this loss *differently*? Could we explore what tiny, survivable moments of leaning into the grief might look like—with you always deciding when to come up for air?

It's not just the grief. It's the *anger* too—like a fire in my chest when I think of all the things left unsaid. How do you carry *that* without burning up inside?

therapist:
I hear how the grief and anger feel like tidal waves and fire—utterly consuming, with no guarantee you'll recognize yourself afterward. That fear of being changed by this pain is so valid; loss *does* reshape us, but not necessarily in ways that erase who you are at your core.  

When you imagine the "you" on the other side of this, what's one quality—maybe even one your dad loved about you—that you *hope* might still remain, no matter how the grief transforms you?

client: I don't know... I guess my stubbornness? Dad always said I was like a dog with a bone when I set my mind to something. But that feels stupid to say now—like it matters at all when he's gone. And what if grief turns even that into something bitter instead? I don't trust that anything good can survive this.
therapist:
It sounds like you're holding onto that stubbornness—that "dog with a bone" quality—even as you fear it might turn bitter in the face of such deep loss. That fear makes so much sense, but I wonder if your dad saw that trait as something strong and enduring, not something grief could easily take away.  

What if, instead of trusting the grief itself right now, you trusted *that part of you*—the part he admired—to guide you through, even when it feels impossible?
